records.text:
Richly-throned immortal Aphrodite,
child of Zeus, weaver of wiles, I beseech you,
do not with anguish nor with sorrows crush,
lady, my heart,
but come hither, if ever at another time too
my voice, hearing it from afar,
you heeded, and leaving your father’s house,
golden, you came,
having yoked your chariot; and fair ones brought you,
swift sparrows, over the black earth
whirling their close-set wings, from heaven through the mid-
air;
and swiftly they arrived; and you, O blessed one,
smiling with your immortal face,
asked what again I had suffered and why
again I was calling,
and what I most wished to happen for me
in my maddened heart: ‘Whom again am I to persuade
to lead you back into her love? Who, O
Sappho, wrongs you?
For if she flees, soon she will pursue;
and if she does not accept gifts, yet she will give them;
and if she does not love, soon she will love
even against her will.’
Come to me now too, and from harsh
cares release me, and all that for me to be accomplished
my heart longs for, accomplish; and you yourself
be my ally.
records.note: Hymn to Aphrodite (the only poem of Sappho preserved complete).

Some say a host of horsemen, others of foot-soldiers,
others of ships, upon the black earth
is the most beautiful thing; but I say it is that
which one loves.
Wholly easy it is to make this understood
by everyone; for she who far surpassed
mankind in beauty, Helen, her husband,
the noblest of all,
left behind and went sailing to Troy,
and neither of her child nor of her dear parents
at all took thought, but led her astray

to be, that man, whoever opposite you
sits and close by, as you sweetly speak,
listens
and as you laugh desirably, which truly

fire at once has run beneath my skin,
and with my eyes I see nothing, and my ears
hum,
and cold sweat holds me down, and trembling
seizes me all over, and greener than grass
I am, and little short of dying

records.note: ‘He seems to me equal to the gods’ (quoted by ‘Longinus’).

But when you are dead you will lie there, nor ever any memory of you
will there be, nor any longing afterwards; for you have no share in the roses
of Pieria, but unseen in the house of Hades too
you will roam among the shadowy dead, flown away from here.
records.note: To an uncultured woman.

As the story goes, because of evil deeds a bitter grief
to Priam and his sons once, Helen, came
from you, and with fire Zeus destroyed
holy Ilium.
Not such was she whom the noble son of Aeacus,
having invited all the blessed gods to the wedding,
led, taking her from the halls of Nereus,
a delicate maiden,
to the house of Chiron; and he loosed the pure
maiden’s girdle; and love flourished
between Peleus and the best of the Nereids,
and within the year
she bore a son, the mightiest of demigods,
a blessed driver of chestnut horses;
but they perished for Helen’s sake, the Phrygians
and their city.
records.note: Helen contrasted with Thetis; the marriage of Peleus and Thetis.

Come now, bring us, boy,
the bowl, so that in one draught
I may drink it down, pouring in ten ladles
of water, and five of wine,
cupfuls, so that without outrage
once again I may play the Bacchant.
Come, once again let us no longer thus
with crashing and shouting
the Scythian way of drinking over wine
practise, but with fair
songs, drinking in moderation.
records.note: Drinking-song in two parts (a, b): the proper mixture of wine and water; no Scythian drinking.

lines.english: Lord, with whom the tamer Eros

and radiant Aphrodite

the high peaks of the mountains:
I beseech you by your knees; and do you graciously
come to us, and to a pleasing
prayer give ear;
to Cleobulus become a good
counsellor, so that my
love, O Dionysus, he may accept.

records.text:
Lord, with whom the tamer Eros
and the dark-eyed Nymphs
and radiant Aphrodite
play together, and who range over
the high peaks of the mountains:
I beseech you by your knees; and do you graciously
come to us, and to a pleasing
prayer give ear;
to Cleobulus become a good
counsellor, so that my
love, O Dionysus, he may accept.
records.note: Prayer to Dionysus for help in a love-affair with Cleobulus.

With a purple ball once again me
striking, golden-haired Eros
with a girl in embroidered sandals
challenges me to play;
but she, for she is from well-built
Lesbos, my hair,
since it is white, finds fault with,
and gapes after some other.

Lifted up once again from the Leucadian
rock into the grey wave I dive, drunk with love.

lines.greek: πρὶν μὲν ἔχων βερβέριον, καλύμματ’ ἐσφηκωμένα,
lines.english: Before, he went about with a berberion, wasp-waisted coverings,

lines.greek: καὶ ξυλίνους ἀστραγάλους ἐν ὠσὶ καὶ ψιλὸν περὶ
lines.english: and wooden dice in his ears, and round
his ribs ‹he wore› a bare hide of ox,
the unwashed wrapping of a wretched shield, with bread-women
and willing whores consorting, the knavish Artemon,
finding himself a counterfeit livelihood,

lines.greek: πολλὰ μὲν ἐν δουρὶ τιθεὶς αὐχένα, πολλὰ δ’ ἐν τροχῷ,
lines.english: often in the stocks putting his neck, often on the wheel,

lines.greek: πολλὰ δὲ νῶτον σκυτίνῃ μάστιγι θωμιχθείς, κόμην
lines.english: often on the back with a leather whip lashed, his hair
and beard plucked out;

lines.greek: νῦν δ’ ἐπιβαίνει σατινέων χρύσεα φορέων κατέρματα
lines.english: but now he mounts carriages, wearing golden earrings,
†the son of Cyce†, and an ivory parasol carries,
just like women ‹in appearance›.

records.text:
Before, he went about with a berberion, wasp-waisted coverings,
and wooden dice in his ears, and round
his ribs ‹he wore› a bare hide of ox,
the unwashed wrapping of a wretched shield, with bread-women
and willing whores consorting, the knavish Artemon,
finding himself a counterfeit livelihood,
often in the stocks putting his neck, often on the wheel,
often on the back with a leather whip lashed, his hair
and beard plucked out;
but now he mounts carriages, wearing golden earrings,
†the son of Cyce†, and an ivory parasol carries,
just like women ‹in appearance›.
records.note: Invective against the upstart Artemon.

lines.english: Grey already are our
temples, and our head white,
graceful youth no longer
is with us, and aged are our teeth,
and of sweet life no longer much
time is left;
for this reason I sob
often, fearing Tartarus;
for Hades’ is a dreadful
recess, and painful into it
is the way down; and indeed it is fixed
for him who has gone down not to come up.

records.text:

and of sweet life no longer much

for this reason I sob
often, fearing Tartarus;
for Hades’ is a dreadful
recess, and painful into it
is the way down; and indeed it is fixed

lines.greek: φέρ’ ὕδωρ φέρ’ οἶνον ὦ παῖ φέρε ⟨δ’⟩ ἀνθεμόεντας ἡμὶν
lines.english: Bring water, bring wine, boy, bring us flowery

lines.greek: στεφάνους· ἔνεικον, ὡς δὴ πρὸς Ἔρωτα πυκταλίζω.
lines.english: garlands; fetch them, so that against Eros I may box.

records.text:
Bring water, bring wine, boy, bring us flowery
garlands; fetch them, so that against Eros I may box.

lines.english: The dice of Eros are
madnesses and uproars.

records.text:
The dice of Eros are
madnesses and uproars.

lines.english: Gently, like a new-born fawn

lines.greek: γαλαθηνὸν ὅς τ’ ἐν ὕλῃ κεροέσσης
lines.english: still suckling, which in the wood by its horned
mother left behind is frightened.

records.text:
Gently, like a new-born fawn
still suckling, which in the wood by its horned
mother left behind is frightened.
records.note: Simile, probably of a timid beloved.

lines.greek: μεγάλῳ δηὖτέ μ’ Ἔρως ἔκοψεν ὥστε χαλκεὺς
lines.english: Once again Eros has struck me like a smith with a great

lines.greek: πελέκει, χειμερίῃ δ’ ἔλουσεν ἐν χαράδρῃ.
lines.english: axe, and has washed me in a wintry torrent.

records.text:
Once again Eros has struck me like a smith with a great
axe, and has washed me in a wintry torrent.

lines.greek: πῶλε Θρῃκίη, τί δή με λοξὸν ὄμμασι βλέπουσα
lines.english: Thracian filly, why, looking askance at me with your eyes,

lines.greek: νηλέως φεύγεις, δοκεῖς δέ μ’ οὐδὲν εἰδέναι σοφόν;
lines.english: do you pitilessly flee, and think I know nothing skilful?

lines.greek: ἴσθι τοι, καλῶς μὲν ἄν τοι τὸν χαλινὸν ἐμβάλοιμι,
lines.english: Know well: I could neatly put the bit on you,

lines.greek: ἡνίας δ’ ἔχων στρέφοιμί σ’ ἀμφὶ τέρματα δρόμου·
lines.english: and holding the reins turn you round the turning-posts of the course;

lines.greek: νῦν δὲ λειμῶνάς τε βόσκεαι κοῦφά τε σκιρτῶσα παίζεις·
lines.english: but now you graze the meadows and play, skipping lightly;

lines.greek: δεξιὸν γὰρ ἱπποπείρην οὐκ ἔχεις ἐπεμβάτην.
lines.english: for you have no skilled horse-breaking rider to mount you.

lines.greek: ἀλκίμων σ’ ὦ ’ριστοκλείδη πρῶτον οἰκτίρω φίλων·
lines.english: Of my valiant friends you, Aristocleides, first I pity;

lines.greek: ὤλεσας δ’ ἥβην ἀμύνων πατρίδος δουληΐην.
lines.english: you lost your youth warding off slavery from your fatherland.

records.text:
Of my valiant friends you, Aristocleides, first I pity;
you lost your youth warding off slavery from your fatherland.

lines.greek: οὐ φιλέω ὃς κρητῆρι παρὰ πλέῳ οἰνοποτάζων
lines.english: I do not love the man who, drinking wine beside the full mixing-bowl,
speaks of quarrels and tearful war,

lines.greek: ἀλλ’ ὅστις Μουσέων τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρ’ Ἀφροδίτης
lines.english: but him who, the Muses’ and Aphrodite’s splendid gifts
mingling, remembers lovely good cheer.

records.text:
I do not love the man who, drinking wine beside the full mixing-bowl,
speaks of quarrels and tearful war,
but him who, the Muses’ and Aphrodite’s splendid gifts
mingling, remembers lovely good cheer.
records.note: Elegiac couplets.
